newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa's ANC urges agreement on new labour laws.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa's ANC urges agreement on new labour laws.

text.p: The African National Congress (ANC) on Monday urged business and labour to resolve their differences over proposed new employment legislation.
The party's national executive committee said in a statement there were "significant areas" of agreement between workers and employers on the Basic Conditions of Employment Bill.

But the ANC committee, the party's decision-making body, said it was concerned that if negotiations were to fail, "the bill may need to be withdrawn and that this would only be to the detriment of the most vulnerable and unprotected workers".

The ANC said it supported efforts to agree on laws on employment conditions "which accord both with the need to improve workers' conditions and with the objective of creating jobs in the context of economic growth and development".

Deputy President Thabo Mbeki told a news conference the ANC was very keen for agreement to be reached on the bill before it was put to parliament in September. The ruling party did not want to have to push through the legislation, he said.
"This is very important legislation. It puts South Africa among the first or second in the world with regard to working conditions. The country should have consensus around it.
"We would rather avoid a situation where we move ahead as government on this thing because of its fundamental importance," Mbeki said.
Labour Minister Tito Mboweni told reporters he was still optimistic a deal could be reached, but reiterated that a deadlock could lead to withdrawal of the proposed law.

"The willingness of the parties to talk and explore suggests that we will be able to find something. But if we don't find that something, there is a real danger of the bill withering away or indeed being withdrawn," he said.
The proposed law was approved by the cabinet in April but still has to passed by parliament before it can take effect.

It has been the subject of ongoing clashes between labour and business, with the ANC-aligned Congress of South African Trade Unions (Cosatu) staging a one-day national work stoppage on June 2 to press business to revise its position.

The labour federation has threatened fresh national strikes next month to reinforce its demands for a 40-hour working week to be phased in over not more than five years, six months' maternity leave of which at least four are paid and double pay for Sunday work.
Business is concerned about the bill's wide scope and provisions which could raise employment costs to the point of creating obstacles to new jobs.
It has also suggested the bill be linked to the government's planned presidential jobs summit in October.
